draft.title: Needs and wants
card: something a person must have to survive, such as food, water and shelter.
something a person would like to have but can live without, such as a new game or the latest trainers.
To sort an item, ask one question: could the person survive without it? If yes, it is a want. If no, it is a need.
The same item can be either. Water to drink is a need. Bottled water in a fancy brand is a want, because plain water would meet the need.
draft.remember: A need is required to survive. A want is something you would like but can live without.

a.q: Which of these is a need?
opts: Clean water to drink
A new mobile phone
A holiday at the beach
A streaming subscription
a.why: People cannot survive without water, so it is a need. A phone, a holiday and a subscription are things people would like, but they can live without them, so they are wants.
a.clue: Which one could a person not live without?

b.q: Ava lives in Hobart. She buys a warm jacket for winter and also buys a designer jacket she likes more. How should the designer jacket be described?
opts: A want, because a plain warm jacket meets the need
A need, because it keeps her warm in winter
A need, because it costs more than a plain jacket
A want, because jackets are never needs
b.why: Staying warm is a need, but a plain warm jacket already meets it. The designer jacket is something Ava would like, so it is a want. Jackets can be needs, so saying they are never needs is wrong.
b.clue: Would Ava stay warm without the designer jacket?

b.best: A want, because a plain warm jacket meets the need

problems.detail: The distractor 'A want, because jackets are never needs' uses 'never', while the card says the same item 'can' be either. It is meant to be wrong and the why explains this. Still, an absolute word in a distractor can teach students to rule out options by spotting 'never' rather than by knowing the idea.

check.summary: The card, the questions and the explanations are accurate and stay within the needs and wants point. The only issue is minor: one distractor in question b uses 'never', which students can rule out as a word cue rather than by understanding the idea.
